### Beyond Proficient

::: {.meta}
Science MCA-IV, spring 2025. Grades 5, 8, and high school.
:::

Minnesota reports school science performance as a percent proficient. That number turns out to be a near-deterministic function of two things the state also publishes: a school's average scale score and its standard deviation. A model using only those two inputs predicts the reported proficiency rate at r = 0.965.

Which means proficiency rates exaggerate real differences. Two schools nine scale points apart report 17% and 43%.

[See the analysis and dashboard](projects/beyond-proficient/){.view}
:::

### Minnesota Early Learning Scholarships

::: {.meta}
County-level awards across five fiscal years.
:::

Minnesota publishes scholarship awards by county but not the rate at which awarded scholarships go unused. Deriving that rate, and a per-county baseline index, made visible which counties are most exposed to the funding contraction that follows a large one-time appropriation.

[See the analysis and dashboard](projects/early-learning/){.view}
:::
:::

## How I work

When two test series are not comparable, I do not draw a trend line across them, even when the chart would look better for it.

Science MCA-IV replaced MCA-III in 2025 against a different set of standards. There is no valid multi-year science trend in Minnesota right now, and saying that plainly is more useful than pointing at something adjacent. The same goes for suppressed cells, which get counted rather than quietly dropped, and for measures I derive myself, which get labeled as derived.

The reason to be careful about any of this is that teachers have to make decisions with these numbers. A clear picture of what the data supports is worth more to them than a confident one.
